books.n: Nobel laureates on what RCTs actually find in development. Replaces ideology with evidence.
Harford is the patient explainer. Coffee shops, traffic, healthcare — markets demystified.
Behavioural-econ canon. Slow in the middle, but the heuristics chapters reshape how you read your own decisions.
Smith, Marx, Keynes, Schumpeter as people, not equations. Best one-volume history of economic thought.
120 pages. Older than your parents and still the sharpest BS-detector primer in print.
Long. But the r > g argument is the single most-cited piece of econ in the last decade — worth meeting first-hand.
A biography of cancer. Reads like a novel; Pulitzer for a reason.
Pharma trials, homeopathy, nutritionists. The book that calibrates your evidence radar for the rest of your life.

books.t: Stiff: The Curious Lives of Human Cadavers
books.n: Roach is gleefully irreverent. Anything she writes is a pleasant read; this is her best.
Theranos, from the WSJ reporter who broke it. Pure thriller pacing.
On aging, end-of-life care, and what medicine quietly gets wrong about both.
Neurosurgeon writes a memoir while dying of lung cancer. Short, devastating, beautiful.
If Emperor lands, this is the companion — heredity from Mendel to CRISPR.
How languages mutate, split, and die. (You're already on this — keeping it as the anchor.)
Sapir–Whorf done responsibly. Does the language you speak change what you see? Sometimes — here's the careful answer.
Where grammar comes from. The 'erosion + creativity' model of linguistic change made vivid.
Linguistics of texting, emoji, lol. Modern, funny, surprisingly rigorous.
More McWhorter — semantic drift, why 'literally' doesn't mean what it used to, and why that's fine.
The Chomskyan case for innate grammar. Contested, but the default starting point.
An AI companion narrates. Ishiguro at the intersection of his Nobel-prose and a near-future setting.
Quiet dystopia. The genre-mechanics are sci-fi but the book is pure literary grief.
A small life, told with unfashionable seriousness. Reissued in 2006 and quietly became a cult favourite.
Russian aristocrat sentenced to lifelong house arrest in the Metropol hotel. Pleasant in the truest sense.
Murakami's most grounded novel — no talking cats, just Tokyo, loss, and a 19-year-old narrator.
Four generations of a Korean family in Japan. Quietly the best historical novel of the last decade.
A communist spy embedded with South Vietnamese refugees in LA. Pulitzer; very funny in unexpected places.

books.t: Stories of Your Life and Others
books.n: Near-perfect short stories. The title piece became Arrival; every other story is at least as good.
Second Chiang collection. Read both — there is nothing else like him working today.
Hard SF on consciousness and first contact. Will mess with you for a week after.
And the two sequels. Scale escalates from Cultural Revolution to heat death of the universe.
Pure pleasant. The Martian guy doing first-contact-via-engineering. Weekend read.
Soviet sci-fi. Short, atmospheric, the source for Stalker — both film and game.
Raises the ceiling on how weird simulation-hypothesis fiction can get. Egan is rigorous and unforgiving.
Canterbury Tales in space. Each pilgrim's story is its own genre.
Uplifted spiders, deep time, surprisingly tender. Don't be put off by the premise.
~250 pages, one sitting, gorgeous. Start here.
If Piranesi lands, go long. Regency England with magic, written in pitch-perfect Austen pastiche.
Cozy court politics, standalone, kind-hearted. A counterweight to grimdark fantasy.
First of the Broken Earth trilogy. Three consecutive Hugos — deserved.
Heist fantasy in a Venice-flavoured city. Comfort read.
Mulan-adjacent retelling of the founder of the Ming dynasty. Sharper than it sounds.
Short, slim, the original 'magic school' before that became a genre. Le Guin is always worth the time.
Sanderson's tightly-engineered magic systems are the gateway drug for many. Start here.
